prompt: Besides carbon, which atoms commonly found in organic molecules can be chirality centers?

choices.text: Nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur
Only nitrogen
choices.why: Trivalent phosphorus (phosphines) and trivalent sulfur (sulfonium salts) can also be chirality centers, and their enantiomers are easier to isolate than those of amines.

choices.text: None; only carbon can be a chirality center
choices.why: The usual requirement is four different substituents on a tetrahedral atom. That atom is usually carbon, but it doesn't have to be.

choices.text: Oxygen and the halogens
choices.why: A chirality center needs four different substituents on a tetrahedral atom, counting a lone pair as one. The atoms commonly found as chirality centers besides carbon are nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur.

explanation: The most common cause of chirality is four different substituents bonded to a tetrahedral atom. Although that atom is usually carbon, it doesn't have to be: nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur atoms are all commonly encountered in organic molecules and can all be chirality centers.

prompt: A trivalent nitrogen, as in an amine, has only three atoms bonded to it. What acts as its fourth "substituent" when you consider it as a possible chirality center?

choices.text: Its lone pair of electrons
A hydrogen atom that every amine carries
choices.why: Not every amine has an N–H bond, and the three bonded atoms are already counted. The fourth position of the tetrahedron is the lone pair.

choices.text: Nothing; trivalent nitrogen is planar, so it can't be a chirality center
choices.why: Trivalent nitrogen is tetrahedral, with its lone pair in the fourth position.

choices.text: An empty orbital
choices.why: Nitrogen in an amine has a filled lone-pair orbital, not an empty one.

explanation: Trivalent nitrogen is tetrahedral, with its lone pair of electrons acting as the fourth "substituent" (Section 1.11). So in principle an amine with three different groups, such as ethylmethylamine, has four different substituents at nitrogen.

prompt: Can ethylmethylamine, CH3NHCH2CH3, be isolated as a pair of enantiomers?

choices.text: Yes in principle, but no in practice: rapid inversion at nitrogen interconverts the enantiomers
Yes; the enantiomers are configurationally stable and can be separated
choices.why: Most trivalent nitrogen compounds undergo a rapid umbrella-like inversion, so individual enantiomers can't be isolated except in special cases.

choices.text: No, because the nitrogen has only three substituents
choices.why: With the lone pair as the fourth substituent, the nitrogen has four different groups (H, CH3, CH2CH3, lone pair), so the molecule is chiral in principle.

choices.text: No, because the molecule has a plane of symmetry
choices.why: Counting the lone pair, the nitrogen carries four different groups, so the molecule is chiral in principle. The problem is that its two enantiomers interconvert rapidly.

explanation: The answer is both yes and no: yes in principle, but no in practice. Most trivalent nitrogen compounds undergo a rapid umbrella-like inversion that interconverts enantiomers, so we can't isolate individual enantiomers except in special cases.

prompt: What process interconverts the two enantiomers of a chiral trivalent nitrogen compound?

choices.text: A rapid umbrella-like inversion at nitrogen
Breaking and re-forming one of the bonds to nitrogen
choices.why: No bonds break. The nitrogen turns inside out, like an umbrella, through its lone pair.

choices.text: Rotation of the molecule by 180°
choices.why: Rotating a molecule never turns it into its enantiomer; enantiomers are nonsuperimposable.

choices.text: Slow inversion that takes several hours at 100 °C
choices.why: That slow rate describes phosphines such as methylpropylphenylphosphine. Inversion at nitrogen is rapid.

explanation: Most trivalent nitrogen compounds undergo a rapid umbrella-like inversion that interconverts enantiomers, so individual enantiomers can't be isolated except in special cases.

prompt: Why can stable chiral phosphines (R3P) be isolated, when most chiral amines (R3N) cannot?

choices.text: Inversion at phosphorus is substantially slower than inversion at nitrogen
Phosphorus has no lone pair, so it cannot invert
choices.why: Trivalent phosphorus does have a lone pair, which counts as its fourth, lowest-ranked substituent. It still inverts, just slowly.

choices.text: Phosphines are planar, so their enantiomers don't interconvert
choices.why: Phosphines, like amines, are tetrahedral with a lone pair in the fourth position; that is what makes them chiral.

choices.text: Phosphorus forms four bonds, while nitrogen forms three
choices.why: A phosphine is trivalent, like an amine: three groups and a lone pair. The difference is the rate of inversion.

explanation: Trivalent phosphorus compounds (phosphines) also undergo inversion, but the inversion at phosphorus is substantially slower than inversion at nitrogen, so stable chiral phosphines can be isolated.

prompt: (R)- and (S)-methylpropylphenylphosphine are configurationally stable for several hours at what temperature, in °C?
explanation: (R)- and (S)-methylpropylphenylphosphine are configurationally stable for several hours at 100 °C, because inversion at phosphorus is substantially slower than inversion at nitrogen.

prompt: When you assign R or S to the phosphorus of methylpropylphenylphosphine, how does its lone pair rank?

choices.text: Lowest of the four substituents
Highest, because it is closest to the phosphorus
choices.why: A lone pair has no atom at all, so it ranks below any group attached through an atom.

choices.text: It isn't ranked; only the three groups bonded to phosphorus are considered
choices.why: The lone pair is the fourth substituent of the tetrahedral phosphorus and is included, as the lowest-ranked group.

choices.text: Between the methyl and propyl groups
choices.why: The lone pair ranks below every one of the three carbon groups.

explanation: In the structure of (R)-methylpropylphenylphosphine, the lone-pair lobe on phosphorus is labeled lowest ranked. Like the lone pair on a trivalent nitrogen, it acts as the fourth substituent.

prompt: Which sulfur compounds can be chiral at sulfur?

choices.text: Trivalent sulfonium salts, R3S+
Divalent sulfur compounds, R2S
choices.why: Divalent sulfur compounds are achiral; the sulfur needs three groups, as in a sulfonium salt.

choices.text: All organic sulfur compounds
choices.why: Divalent sulfur compounds are achiral at sulfur. Only trivalent sulfur, in sulfonium salts, can be chiral.

choices.text: None; sulfur atoms can't be chirality centers
choices.why: Sulfonium salts can be chiral and configurationally stable, like S-adenosylmethionine.

explanation: Divalent sulfur compounds are achiral, but trivalent sulfur compounds called sulfonium salts (R3S+) can be chiral.

prompt: Why can chiral sulfonium salts be isolated as single enantiomers?

choices.text: Like phosphines, they undergo relatively slow inversion, so they are configurationally stable
Sulfur can't invert at all
choices.why: Sulfonium salts do invert, but relatively slowly; S-adenosylmethionine is stable for several days at room temperature, not forever.

choices.text: Like amines, they undergo rapid inversion
choices.why: Rapid inversion is what prevents the isolation of chiral amines. Sulfonium salts invert slowly.

choices.text: Their positive charge makes them achiral
choices.why: The charge doesn't remove chirality; sulfonium salts with three different groups are chiral.

explanation: Like phosphines, sulfonium salts undergo relatively slow inversion, so chiral sulfonium salts are configurationally stable and can be isolated.

prompt: What is the biological role of S-adenosylmethionine, the best-known chiral sulfonium salt?

choices.text: It is the biological methyl donor, a source of CH3 groups in many metabolic pathways
It is used in the laboratory to resolve racemic carboxylic acids
choices.why: Resolution of acids uses chiral amines such as 1-phenylethylamine. S-Adenosylmethionine is a coenzyme.

choices.text: It is a chiral phosphine used in amino acid synthesis
choices.why: It contains a sulfonium sulfur, not phosphorus. Chiral phosphines are the ones the book links to amino acid synthesis (Section 26.3).

choices.text: It is a source of sulfur atoms for building proteins
choices.why: The section describes it as a source of CH3 groups, the so-called biological methyl donor.

explanation: The coenzyme S-adenosylmethionine is the so-called biological methyl donor, involved in many metabolic pathways as a source of CH3 groups.

prompt: What does the "S" in the name S-adenosylmethionine mean?

choices.text: Sulfur: the adenosyl group is attached to the sulfur atom of methionine
The S configuration at the sulfur
choices.why: The molecule does have S stereochemistry at sulfur, but the "S" in the name stands for sulfur, the atom that carries the adenosyl group.

choices.text: Sinister, meaning it is the levorotatory form
choices.why: The name's "S" is the atom sulfur. Neither R/S labels nor the name tell you the sign of optical rotation.

choices.text: Salt, because it is a sulfonium salt
choices.why: It is a sulfonium salt, but the "S" marks where the adenosyl group is attached: the sulfur atom.

explanation: The "S" in the name S-adenosylmethionine stands for sulfur and means that the adenosyl group is attached to the sulfur atom of the amino acid methionine. (Separately, the molecule happens to have S stereochemistry at that sulfur.)

prompt: Which statement about the stereochemistry of biologically active S-adenosylmethionine is correct?

choices.text: It has S stereochemistry at sulfur and is configurationally stable for several days at room temperature
It has R stereochemistry at sulfur; the S enantiomer is not biologically active
choices.why: It is the other way around: the active coenzyme is S at sulfur, and its R enantiomer is known but not biologically active.

choices.text: It is a racemic mixture, because sulfur inverts rapidly
choices.why: Sulfonium salts invert relatively slowly. The S form is stable for several days at room temperature.

choices.text: It is achiral at sulfur, because divalent sulfur is achiral
choices.why: Its sulfur carries three groups (a sulfonium salt), not two, so it can be chiral.

explanation: S-Adenosylmethionine has S stereochemistry at sulfur and is configurationally stable for several days at room temperature. Its R enantiomer is also known but is not biologically active.

prompt: Which of these compounds could be isolated as a single, configurationally stable enantiomer?

choices.text: (R)-Methylpropylphenylphosphine, CH3(CH3CH2CH2)(C6H5)P
(R)-Ethylmethylpropylamine, CH3(CH3CH2)(CH3CH2CH2)N
choices.why: Its nitrogen has four different substituents counting the lone pair, but rapid umbrella-like inversion interconverts the enantiomers.

choices.text: Ethyl methyl sulfide, CH3SCH2CH3
choices.why: Divalent sulfur compounds are achiral, so there is no enantiomer to isolate.

choices.text: Ethylmethylamine, CH3NHCH2CH3
choices.why: It is chiral in principle, but rapid inversion at nitrogen interconverts its enantiomers.

explanation: Inversion at phosphorus is substantially slower than at nitrogen, so chiral phosphines such as methylpropylphenylphosphine are configurationally stable (for several hours at 100 °C). Most amines invert rapidly, and divalent sulfur compounds are achiral.
